questions.q: The subcortex tree: grey matter and white matter give rise to which structures?
opts: Basal ganglia; corticospinal tract and corticobulbar fibres passing through the internal capsule
questions.exp: Subcortex -> grey matter -> basal ganglion; white matter -> corticospinal tract, corticobulbar fibres (pass through internal capsule). (Book p583)

questions.q: Per the nuclei diagram, the corpus striatum and lenticular nucleus are formed by which pairings?
questions.exp: Nuclei: caudate nucleus (CN), putamen, globus pallidus (GP: GPi, GPe), subthalamic nucleus (STN), substantia nigra (SN); corpus striatum = CN + putamen; lenticular nucleus = putamen + GP. (Book p583)

questions.q: A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus produces which movement disorder per the diagram?
questions.exp: Lesion -> hypokinetic movements: caudate -> chorea; putamen/striatum -> dystonia/athetosis; STN -> hemiballismus. (Book p583)

questions.q: The basal-ganglia physiology functions listed are:
opts: Respiratory drive, heart rate, blood pressure
Complex motor activity; initiation and scaling of movement; cognitive part; activity set for movement (planning, programming, initiation)
Sensory discrimination, memory consolidation, language naming
questions.exp: Functions: complex motor activity; initiation and scaling of movement; cognitive part of motor activity; activity set for movement (planning, programming and initiation). Note: premotor cortex and supplementary motor area also involved in planning and programming. (Book p583)

questions.q: The three general features of the direct and indirect pathways are:
opts: All input from thalamus; output via STN; only inhibitory nucleus is GPi
Input from brainstem; output via SN; only excitatory is caudate
All input from cerebellum; output via thalamus; subthalamus inhibitory
All input from cortex to striatum; all output leaves through GPi; the only excitatory BG nucleus is the subthalamus
questions.exp: General features: 1. all input from cortex -> striatum; 2. all output leave through GPi; 3. the only excitatory nucleus in BG: subthalamus. (Book p584)

questions.q: The nigrostriatal pathway (SN -> corpus striatum) acts via D1 and D2 receptors to do what?
opts: D1 activates the direct pathway and D2 inhibits the indirect pathway, together stimulating the cortex
D1 inhibits the direct pathway and D2 activates the indirect pathway
D1 excites STN and D2 excites GPe
questions.exp: Nigrostriatal pathway: via D1 activate direct pathway; via D2 inhibits indirect pathway - together stimulating of cortex. (Book p584)

questions.q: Degeneration of the nigrostriatal pathway in PD produces which applied-aspect outcome?
opts: Inhibition of the cortex -> akinesia and bradyphrenia (slowness of thoughts)
questions.exp: Applied aspect: degeneration of NS pathway (Parkinson's disease) -> inhibition of cortex -> akinesia, bradyphrenia (slowness of thoughts). Disorders of BG: hyperkinetic vs hypokinetic (paucity of movement - down amplitude, slowness - unrelated to weakness/spasticity). Idiopathic PD: and m/c neurodegenerative disease; majority cases sporadic, elderly > 60 years. (Book p584)

questions.q: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: the majority cases are which distribution and age?
questions.exp: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease: and m/c neurodegenerative disease; majority cases: distribution sporadic, age elderly > 60 years. (Book p584)

questions.q: The 'typical symptomatic appearance' figure labels which constellation?
opts: Hyperextended posture, lively facies, flaccidity, wide-based ataxic gait
Forward lean with brisk arm swing and long strides

Stooped posture, masked facial expression, rigidity, forward tilt of trunk, flexed elbows and wrists, reduced arm swinging, slightly flexed hips and knees, trembling of extremities, shuffling short-stepped gait
questions.exp: Figure labels: stooped posture, masked facial expression, rigidity, forward tilt of trunk, flexed elbows and wrists, reduced arm swinging, slightly flexed hips and knees, trembling of extremities, shuffling short-stepped gait. (Book p585)

questions.q: The tremor-comparison table gives Parkinson disease tremor frequency as:
questions.exp: Frequency row: PD tremor 4-6 Hz; essential tremor 5-12 Hz. (Book p585)

questions.q: A rest tremor with re-emergent component, asymmetric, hands and legs, micrographia, progressive course, 1% family history, extrapyramidal signs present, levodopa-responsive, DBS at STN or GPi - which tremor?
questions.exp: PD column: at rest +/- re-emergent tremor, asymmetric, hands +/- legs, small writing (micrographia), progressive, family history uncommon (1%), extrapyramidal signs (bradykinesia, rigidity, loss of postural reflex) present, relieved by levodopa/dopamine agonists/anticholinergics, DBS site subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna. Essential column: postural tremor, mostly symmetric, hands/head/voice, large and tremulous writing, stable or slowly progressive, family history common (>30%), EPS absent, relieved by alcohol/propranolol/primidone/topiramate/gabapentin/clonazepam, DBS ventral intermediate thalamus. (Book p585)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the relieving factor NOT for Parkinson disease tremor per the table:
questions.exp: PD relieving factors: levodopa, dopamine agonists, anticholinergics; essential tremor relieving factors include alcohol, propranolol, primidone, topiramate, gabapentin, clonazepam. (Book p585)

questions.q: The sheet for printed p586 is absent from the supplied scan. Which statement correctly places it in the Parkinson's sequence?
opts: It lies between the p583 title page and the p584 pathway diagram
It lies between the p589 L-dopa list and the p592 agonist examples
No sheet is missing - p587 follows p585 directly in the scan
It lies between the p585 tremor-comparison table and the p587 rigidity list
questions.exp: Printed p586 is absent from the supplied scan (it proceeds p585 -> p587); its bracketing content is the p585 PD-versus-essential tremor table and the p587 rigidity/akinesia list. Content verification of p586 remains unresolved, as with the missing p527 in Chapter 26. (Book p586)

questions.q: Cogwheel and lead-pipe rigidity are distinguished at which sites per the page, and what is Froment's sign?
opts: Cogwheel (rigidity + tremor) at the wrist; lead pipe at the elbow; Froment's sign = activity-induced increase in c/l rigidity
Cogwheel at the elbow; lead pipe at the wrist; Froment's sign = thumb pinch sign
Both at the ankle; Froment's sign = falling backwards
Both at the neck; Froment's sign = tremor vanishing in action
questions.exp: Hypertonia - 2 types: cogwheel rigidity (rigidity + tremor) at wrist; lead pipe rigidity at elbow. Froment's sign: activity-induced increase in c/l rigidity (as printed on the page). (Book p587)

questions.q: Bradyphrenia, reduced arm swing, stooped posture from flexion hypertonia, short quick steps with freezing, narrow-based festinant gait, micrographia, hypomimia, hypophonia and reduced blinking - this printed cluster is:
questions.exp: Akinesia/bradykinesia: bradyphrenia; reduced arm swing (difficulty with limb movements); flexion hypertonia (stooped posture); short quick steps and freeze in between; festinant gait (narrow-based); micrographia; hypomimia (minimal expression); hypophonia (down voice); reduced blinking - glabellar tap sign positive. (Book p587)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the item NOT on the atypical-PD/hypokinesia note on this page:
questions.exp: Note: atypical PD - b/l axial rigidity: difficulty turning in bed, rising from a chair (wheelchair sign); non-parkinsonian lesion having hypokinesia: hypothyroidism. (Visual hallucinations with fluctuating alertness are DLB features on p588.) (Book p587)

questions.q: The pull test shows the patient falls backward (normal: takes 2-3 steps backwards to correct posture) - which feature is demonstrated?
questions.exp: Postural instability: unsteadiness and falls; pull test - patient falls backward (normal: takes 2-3 steps backwards to correct posture). (Book p587)

questions.q: The investigation line for Parkinson's disease states the diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Investigation: clinical diagnosis. (Book p587)

questions.q: MRI at midbrain level shows b/l grey-matter hyperintensities surrounded by hypointense red nuclei and crural fibres, with absent swallow-tail sign - the sign's origin per the note is:
opts: The substantia nigra (swallow tail sign d/t SN)
questions.exp: MRI midbrain level: hyperintensities b/l in grey matter surrounded by hypointense red nuclei and crural fibres; absence of swallow tail sign (swallow tail sign d/t SN). (Book p587)

questions.q: The 'PD patient can also have' note lists which symptom groups?
questions.exp: PD patients can also have sensory symptoms (pain, anosmia), neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression > dementia) and gastrointestinal symptoms (dysphagia). (Book p587)

questions.q: Atypical Parkinson's disease is also called what, with which listed hallmarks?
opts: Parkinson minus syndromes - slow progression, late dementia
Parkinson plus syndromes - rapid progression, early onset dementia, symmetrical bradykinesia, facial dyskinesia
questions.exp: Atypical PD aka Parkinson plus syndromes: rapid progression, early onset dementia, symmetrical bradykinesia, facial dyskinesia. Classifications: tauopathy (PSP, CBD) and alpha synucleinopathy (MSA, DLB). (Book p588)

questions.q: The features common to atypical PD itself per the list are:
opts: Absence of tremor, unresponsiveness to L-dopa, rapidly progressive
Prominent rest tremor, good L-dopa response, slowly progressive
questions.exp: Atypical PD: absence of tremor, unresponsiveness to L-dopa, rapidly progressive; DLB: dementia at presentation, visual hallucination, fluctuating alertness; CBD: myoclonus, cortical signs; PSP: falls d/t postural instability, dementia component, b/l axial rigidity, supranuclear gaze palsy; MSA: ANS symptoms, disproportionate cerebellar signs. (Book p588)

questions.q: Supranuclear gaze palsy with b/l axial rigidity and falls from postural instability - which atypical PD?
questions.exp: PSP: falls d/t postural instability, dementia component, b/l axial rigidity, supranuclear gaze palsy. (Book p588)

questions.q: CBD's listed features are:
questions.exp: CBD: myoclonus, cortical signs; DLB: dementia at presentation, visual hallucination, fluctuating alertness; MSA: ANS symptoms, disproportionate cerebellar signs. (Book p588)

questions.q: MSA per the page: age range and defining inclusions are:
opts: 45-55 years; glial cytoplasmic inclusions staining for alpha synuclein
questions.exp: MSA: 45-55 yrs; glial cytoplasmic inclusions (stain for alpha synuclein) - alpha synucleinopathy; REM sleep disorders (years before diagnosis); ANS predominant. (Book p588)

questions.q: The MSA classification prints what proportion as MSA-P (parkinson predominant)?
questions.exp: MSA classification: MSA-P (80%) parkinson predominant; MSA-C cerebellar predominant; MSA-A/Shy-Drager syndrome (15%) ANS predominant. (Book p588)

questions.q: L-dopa is combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor because:
opts: Peripheral metabolism of L-dopa is high
L-dopa cannot cross the blood-brain barrier without it
questions.exp: Drugs: L-Dopa - peripheral metabolism is high; combined with: dopa decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa, benserazide); COMT inhibitors - not used now: tolcapone (hepatotoxic), entacapone (hepatotoxic, orange coloured urine); L-Dopa + dopa decarboxylase inhibitor is the combination started. (Book p589)

questions.q: The L-dopa administration details printed on the page are:
opts: Only when symptoms are severe, fasting
Small doses, multiple times, crushed and mixed with carbonated water
Single large dose at night with plain water
questions.exp: All patients are started on L-dopa: small doses, multiple times, crushed and mixed with carbonated water. Symptoms non-responsive to L-dopa: freezing, falls, dysphagia, dysarthria, ANS symptoms. (Book p589)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT - the symptom NOT printed as non-responsive to L-dopa:
questions.exp: Symptoms non-responsive to L-dopa: freezing, falls, dysphagia, dysarthria, ANS symptoms. (Book p589)

questions.q: Peak-dose choreiform dyskinesia and off-period dystonia differ by what per the page?
opts: High dose versus low drug concentration respectively
questions.exp: Side effects: nausea/vomiting, postural hypotension; motor fluctuations - wearing off (space drug without much gap), on/off, delayed onset of action, drug failure; dyskinesias - peak dose dyskinesia: choreiform movements (d/t high dose), off period dyskinesia: dystonia (d/t low drug concentration). (Book p589)

questions.q: The drug the page assigns to tackle motor fluctuations is:
questions.exp: Motor fluctuations (wearing off, on/off, delayed onset of action, drug failure) - to tackle: amantadine. (Book p589)

questions.q: Central anticholinergics and the dopaminergic-agonist disadvantage note state:
opts: Propranolol is used in drug-induced PD; DDS brings pain and anosmia
Carbidopa is a central anticholinergic; DDS brings seizures and aphasia
Trihexyphenidyl is used in drug-induced PD; DDS brings visual hallucinations, impulse control issues, addiction
Trihexyphenidyl is the DOC for idiopathic PD; DDS brings depression and amnesia
questions.exp: Central anticholinergics: trihexyphenidyl; used in drug-induced PD. Dopaminergic agonists: found as replacement for L-dopa; disadvantages - dopamine dysregulation syndrome (neuropsychiatric manifestations: visual hallucinations, impulse control issues, addiction). (Book p589)

questions.q: The supplied scan proceeds directly from p589 to p592. What is absent between them?
opts: Nothing is missing - p592 follows p589 in the book
Printed p590 and p591, both missing from the supplied scan
questions.exp: Printed p590 and p591 are absent from the supplied scan, so the dopaminergic-agonist material between the p589 disadvantages list and the p592 examples list cannot be visually verified; this follows the unresolved-missing-page precedent set by p527 in Chapter 26. (Book p590)

questions.q: The p591 sheet is absent from the supplied scan. Which visible page carries the 'Example: pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine' list that follows it?
opts: Printed p592, which opens with that examples list
Printed p589, which ends with the DDS note
questions.exp: With p591 (and p590) absent from the supplied scan, the next visible sheet - p592 - opens with the dopaminergic-agonist examples list: pramipexole (antidepressant action also), ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine (used in rescue therapy, IV route). (Book p591)

questions.q: The dopaminergic-agonist examples list on this page includes which drug used in rescue therapy by the IV route?
questions.exp: Example: pramipexole (antidepressant action also), ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine - i. used in rescue therapy, ii. IV route. (Book p592)

questions.q: Amantadine's printed mechanisms of action number how many, and which are they?
questions.exp: Amantadine: 3 mechanisms of action - dopaminergic agonist, anticholinergic, NMDA antagonist. Newer drugs: istradefylline (A2a antagonist - minimizes motor fluctuations), pimavanserin (5HTa antagonist). (Book p592)

questions.q: The treatment protocol prints which first-line choice for a patient <60 years with mild symptoms?
questions.exp: Treatment protocol: <60 yrs old + mild symptoms -> dopaminergic agonist; >60 yrs / significant disease present -> L-dopa + carbidopa. (Book p592)

The PD-versus-essential tremor table is read row by row; printed p586 is absent from the supplied scan.

The akinesia/bradykinesia cluster, atypical notes, postural instability and the swallow-tail MRI follow.

Parkinson-plus hallmarks and the tau/synuclein classification set the atypical group.
Entity-specific features, then MSA age, inclusions and subtype proportions.

L-dopa, decarboxylase and COMT inhibitors with administration and fluctuation handling.
Anticholinergics and agonist disadvantages; printed p590-p591 are absent from the supplied scan.
The p592 examples, amantadine MOA, newer drugs and the age-based protocol close the chapter.
